title: Collect, use and communicate data that relate to farming

lessons.title: Collecting farm data accurately
lessons.html:
Collecting farm data accurately

Data are facts and numbers. Farms collect data every day: how much rain fell, how many crates were picked, how much milk was produced, which animals were treated, how much diesel was used. Managers use these data to make decisions, pay workers, plan and meet the rules of buyers and the law.

Examples of farm data

AreaData collected
WeatherRainfall (mm), minimum and maximum temperature
CropsPlanting date, cultivar, fertiliser and sprays used, yield
AnimalsBirths, deaths, weights, treatments, milk or eggs produced
LabourHours worked, crates or bins per picker
MachinesHours, fuel used, services
StoresFeed, seed and chemicals in and out

Tools for collecting data

  • Rain gauge, thermometer, scales, measuring tape, counters and meters.
  • Paper forms, notebooks, registers and tally sheets.
  • Cell phone apps and tablets used by many farms.

Rules for good data

  1. Be accurate. Read instruments carefully. Read the rain gauge at eye level and at the same time every day, then empty it.
  2. Be complete. Fill in every column: date, place, who, what, how many, units.
  3. Use the right units. Kilograms, litres, millimetres, hectares. Do not mix them up.
  4. Write clearly. Others must be able to read your numbers. Write 7 and 1 clearly.
  5. Record straight away. Do not rely on memory at the end of the day.
  6. Be honest. Never make up or change numbers. Wrong data leads to wrong decisions, and false records about chemicals or treatments can break the law and lose markets.

If you make a mistake on a paper form, draw one line through it, write the correct number next to it and sign it. Do not use correction fluid.

lessons.title: Using and communicating data
lessons.html:
Using and communicating data

Simple calculations

  • Totals: add up daily figures. Example: milk for the week = Monday + Tuesday + ... + Sunday.
  • Averages: total divided by the number of items. Example: 5 pickers picked 60, 55, 70, 65 and 50 crates. Total = 300. Average = 300 / 5 = 60 crates each.
  • Per hectare: yield divided by area. Example: 24 tonnes from 4 hectares = 6 tonnes per hectare.
  • Percentages: part divided by total x 100. Example: 6 dead out of 200 chickens = 6 / 200 x 100 = 3%.
  • Comparisons: this week against last week, this block against another.

Presenting data

Data are easier to understand in a table or graph.

  • Tables show exact numbers in rows and columns.
  • Bar graphs compare things, such as yield per block.
  • Line graphs show change over time, such as rainfall per month or milk per day.

Always give a heading, label each axis or column and show the units.

Using data to spot problems

Watch for sudden changes. For example:

  • Egg numbers drop: possible disease, heat stress or water problem.
  • Diesel use rises sharply: possible leak, faulty machine or theft.
  • One block yields much less than others: possible pest, soil or irrigation problem.

Report these changes to your supervisor with the numbers.

Communicating data

  • Give the right information to the right person at the right time, for example daily picking totals to the office before the end of the day.
  • Speak clearly and give units: "Block 3 had 42 millimetres of rain last night", not just "42".
  • Hand in forms on time and keep copies where required.
  • Keep personal data, such as workers' ID numbers and wages, private.

Key points

  • Farms collect data on weather, crops, animals, labour, machines and stores.
  • Good data are accurate, complete, in the right units, clear, recorded at once and honest.
  • Use totals, averages, per hectare figures and percentages to understand data.
  • Tables and graphs with headings and units make data easy to read.
  • Report sudden changes and communicate data on time, keeping personal data private.
